title: Measurement Uncertainty
body:
Every measurement produces a range, and the laboratory component of the course is largely about
handling that honestly.

An **uncertainty** states how far the true value might reasonably be from the reading. A length
recorded as $12.4 \pm 0.1$ cm claims that the true value is probably between 12.3 and 12.5. The
uncertainty comes from the instrument's resolution, from the repeatability of the procedure, or
from the spread of repeated trials.

**Significant figures** carry the same claim implicitly. Writing 12.40 asserts more precision
than writing 12.4, so a computed result quoted to eight digits from a measurement good to three
is claiming precision that does not exist.

**Propagation** follows the operation:

```
adding or subtracting     absolute uncertainties add
multiplying or dividing   relative uncertainties add
```

```
12.4 ± 0.1 cm  by  8.2 ± 0.1 cm

  area  = 101.68 cm²
  relative: 0.1/12.4 + 0.1/8.2 = 0.0081 + 0.0122 = 0.0203
  absolute: 0.0203 × 101.68 = 2.1
  report: 102 ± 2 cm²
```

Comparing a measured value against a predicted one means asking whether the two ranges overlap.
That is the same question [[Hypothesis Testing]] asks in [[STATISTICS]] with a probability
attached, and repeated measurements of one quantity scatter according to the
[[Normal Distribution]] with a spread measured by [[Variance]].

Systematic error shifts every reading the same way and is invisible to repetition, so averaging
more trials never removes it. Random error scatters both ways and shrinks with the number of
trials as $1/\sqrt{n}$, which is the [[Central Limit Theorem]] appearing in a
first-year lab.
